# Code style (pokedex Python)

The always-on subset, consolidated from CLAUDE.md and `integration-patterns.md` "Code style". Full reviewer checklist (incl. advisory / new-build-only items like `while True`, guard clauses, inline dict values): `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Code style".

- **No docstrings, with two exceptions.** Pokedex code is self-documenting. Both exceptions are where the docstring is published text, not a comment: `api.py` endpoint handlers, whose docstring is the endpoint's OpenAPI summary and description (the rollout pushes that spec to Mintlify and Svix, so it is the public API docs, and every public endpoint carries one); Alembic migration modules under `migrations/versions/`, which keep the generated header (title, `Revision ID`, `Revises`, `Create Date`) plus a line of rationale when the schema change is not obvious from the operations. Nothing under `integrations/`, `utils/`, `resources/`, or `actions/` has one.
- **Default to no comment; when in doubt, delete.** A comment exists only when the change is not obvious from the code alone. If the code, a variable name, or the error message beside it already says it, the comment is noise — delete it rather than polish it. That covers narration ("sum the quantities per sku"), section labels, and anything restating an assert or a raise.
- **Comments: lowercase, ≤2 lines, why not what.** Vendor quirks, surprising invariants, non-obvious couplings. Vendor field names keep their original casing inside a lowercase comment (`DeliveryNotes` stays `DeliveryNotes`) — lowercasing them breaks the reference. The ceiling yields only when a genuinely non-obvious vendor data model or a disambiguating example needs the room and nothing shorter carries it. The same ceiling applies to raised error messages — a `PokedexException` says what went wrong and what to do in a line or two, not a paragraph.
- **ELI5, no jargon.** Write it the way you'd say it out loud to an engineer new to the codebase: plain words any SWE understands cold, in one read. No noun-stacks ("multi-lot pick collision"), no arrow chains (`x → y → z`), no model-speak ("ensure correctness", "for clarity", "leverage"), no clever compression that needs decoding ("must not look like it did"). "with no batch number, picks from different batches get combined here, so we can't keep a single expiry date" beats "blank-batch multi-lot picks collapse under the package uniqueness key, dropping the expiry anchor".
- **Comments are self-contained.** Never reference `api-summary.md`, any `.claude/...` file, doctrine vocabulary ("tier-3", "shallow-fix", "per integration-patterns"), or the authoring agent. A reader at HEAD with only this file open must understand it.
- **Comments never name** customer orgs, the source integration a pattern was copied from, or observation dates — those leak or rot. The ban is on customers: naming the integration's own vendor inside its own files is normal. Rich rationale (customer, pattern source, load-bearing dates) lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Exception: vendor/3PL support-contact lines inside `support()` — naming contacts is that method's job.
- **Raise, don't `assert`.** Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` exception helpers), never `assert` — asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status or origin. `assert` belongs in tests only.
- **A package `__init__.py` that re-exports lists those names in `__all__`.** Re-exports are the point of the file, but every one of them reads as an unused import to the linter, so the list is what keeps it quiet and doubles as the package's public surface. Add a name in both places or the linter flags it again.
- **No `@property` on anything a subclass overrides.** A value an integration can change is a plain method, so every call site shows it's dispatched rather than read off the instance. `@property` is still fine for something defined once and never overridden (`staging_key`, `bucket`). Name a boolean method for how it reads at the call site — `uses_browserbase()`, not `use_browserbase()`.
- **No `ABC` / `@abstractmethod`.** A base class declares a method subclasses must supply by raising `NotImplementedError` in the body, with a short message saying what the subclass owes. That's the one pattern used everywhere else, and on integrations it's load-bearing: `BaseIntegration.is_implemented` reads a method's source looking for that raise to decide which functions an integration supports, so an abstract stub would be read as implemented and get scheduled.
- **UPPER_CASE names are module-level only.** A constant-style value scoped inside a function is a lowercase local like any other; capitals are reserved for module-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor tunables).
- **No leading-underscore "private" names** on methods, attributes, or locals. Underscore privacy isn't enforced here and signals nothing. If a class helper needs `self` it's a method; if not, hoist it module-level; if used once, inline it. (Dunders like `__init__` are exempt.)
- **Error-driven: avoid `.get()` — on vendor-response reads.** Loud failures (a `KeyError` during `yarn crawl`) are how we learn real API behavior. `.get(field, default)` on a vendor response is allowed only after observing the field is genuinely sometimes-absent. Nullable is not optional: a key the vendor always sends but sometimes nulls is read with a direct index (plus an `or` fallback when a default is needed) — `.get()` there misstates the contract by implying the key can be missing. The rule does not cover reads where absence is the normal, documented case — optional fields of a validated write payload in `create_*`/`update_*` methods, marshmallow `query_data` in API handlers (absent optional params are omitted from the dict), and our own state attributes that most rows don't carry — there `.get()` is the convention and is self-documenting. Comment a `.get()` only when the absence is surprising (the contract says the field should be there and observation proved otherwise: `# vendor returns null for unfulfilled orders`); a `.get()` on a documented-optional field needs no comment.
- **No list/dict comprehensions in integration code.** Use multi-line `for` loops with named intermediates — comprehensions are opaque under `pdb`.
- **No `logger.info` / `print` in integration code** (carrier is the documented exception — its async/queued flows justify checkpoint logging). Every other type stays quiet: Datadog spans + connection-error rows are the observability surface; `logger.warning`/`error` only for genuinely surprising, actionable states.
- **Platform constants live in `config.py`.** Feature modules `import config`; don't scatter `os.environ.get`. Integration-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor base URLs, per-vendor tunables) stay in the integration's own module — they're hard to unify across vendors and don't belong in the shared config.
- **Favor simplicity over cleverness — and the smallest fix that addresses the root cause.** A fix that adds new mechanisms (a helper, a wrapper, a retry layer, config) where editing an existing line suffices is overengineered and gets rejected in review. Before inventing a new shape, check how neighboring integrations already solve the same problem and match it. The same bar applies to edge cases: a narrow race or double-failure edge that self-corrects on the next cycle (or whose outcome is still correct for the user) is documented — or made observable with a log line — not engineered around with new state machines or guards.

- **Reuse the codebase's words; never coin a verb.** A name is found, not composed: before naming a function, helper, constant, status value, or table, grep for how neighbors name the same operation on the same kind of thing (`rg -n 'def \w+_<noun>\b'`, `rg -n 'def \w+_row\b'`) and pick from the verbs that come back; the search is by object, never by a list of verbs, because a list is itself a vocabulary that drifts. Dynamo row helpers are `create_ / get_ / update_ / store_ / delete_<thing>_row`. Under `integrations/`, data-function and action names come from the resource and action contracts, so there is nothing to choose. A status string is the word the API's error text uses for that state (`unconfirmed` when the 409 says "could not be confirmed"), so the row, the log line, and the error read the same. A word from one recent feature is not established vocabulary; count its uses across the repo before adopting it. Payments, ops, and distributed-systems jargon (`settle`, `claim`, `release`, `landed`, `in flight`, `ambiguous`, `reconcile`) is a coined verb here unless the grep shows it already carries that meaning in this codebase. Say what the code does in words the code already uses: `mark_<row>_succeeded`, `store_write_ids_for_replay`, `write_may_have_reached_vendor`.
- **Comments and error messages use the code's own names.** A comment names the function, status, and field exactly as the code spells them and describes the mechanism in the same verbs. A comment that introduces a second vocabulary for the thing beside it is rewritten in the code's words or deleted.

## Running code & tests
- **Tests: only `yarn test` with filters.** Never `python -m pytest` or raw `pytest`. Scopes/markers: `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md`.
- **Ad-hoc Python: `uv run python3`.** Never raw `python3`/`python` — dependencies resolve through `uv`.
